notes.definition: Producers transfer only about 1% of the incident energy from light into biomass by photosynthesis, and only about 10% of the biomass at each trophic level is transferred to the level above. The rest is lost through egestion, excretion and respiration.
explanation: Food chains start with producers, which are mostly plants and algae. Producers use light for photosynthesis, but they transfer only about 1% of the incident energy from light to the glucose and other substances that make up their biomass. This small amount of biomass made by producers is all that is available to every other organism in the food chain.

Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it. For example, if the grass in a field has 10 000 g/m² of biomass, the rabbits feeding on it might have about 1000 g/m², and the foxes feeding on the rabbits about 100 g/m². This explains why pyramids of biomass are pyramid shaped.

Biomass is lost between trophic levels in several ways. First, not all the ingested material is absorbed: some cannot be digested and is egested (passed out) as faeces. Second, some absorbed material is lost as waste. Carbon dioxide and water are produced in respiration and released into the environment, and water and urea are lost in urine. Third, large amounts of the glucose absorbed are used in respiration to release energy for movement, keeping warm and other life processes, so this glucose does not become new body tissue. Not all parts of an organism are eaten either, for example roots or bones.

The efficiency of biomass transfer between trophic levels can be calculated: efficiency = biomass transferred to the next level ÷ biomass available at the previous level × 100. For example, if producers have 2000 g/m² and herbivores 150 g/m², the efficiency is 150 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 7.5%. Efficiency can also be given as a fraction of the mass, for example 150/2000 = 3/40.

Because so much biomass is lost at each step, there is less biomass available at each higher trophic level. This means each level can support fewer organisms (a smaller total mass of organisms) than the level below. It also explains why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels: by then there is too little biomass left to support another population.
keyFacts: Producers transfer about 1% of the incident light energy for photosynthesis.
About 10% of the biomass at each trophic level is transferred to the level above.
Not all ingested material is absorbed: some is egested as faeces.
Some absorbed material is lost as waste: carbon dioxide and water from respiration, water and urea in urine.
Large amounts of glucose are used in respiration, so they do not become new biomass.
Efficiency can be given as a percentage or as a fraction of the mass.
Less biomass at each level means fewer organisms can be supported at higher trophic levels.

keyTerms.definition: The mass of living material in an organism or group of organisms.
The light energy falling on a producer, of which only about 1% is transferred by photosynthesis.
Passing out undigested, unabsorbed food from the gut as faeces.
Removal of waste products made in the body, such as urea in urine and carbon dioxide from respiration.
The percentage (or fraction) of the biomass at one trophic level that is transferred to the next level.

equations.name: Efficiency of biomass transfer
equations.formula: efficiency (%) = biomass transferred to the next level ÷ biomass available at the previous level × 100
equations.symbols: efficiency = (biomass in higher level ÷ biomass in lower level) × 100
equations.units: percentage (%), or a fraction with no units

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that the 90% of biomass not transferred is 'used up' or destroyed.
misconceptions.right: In fact it leaves the food chain as specific losses: undigested material egested as faeces, carbon dioxide and water from respiration, water and urea in urine, and parts of organisms that are not eaten.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse the 1% and 10% figures.
misconceptions.right: In fact about 1% is the proportion of incident light energy producers transfer by photosynthesis, while about 10% is the proportion of biomass passed from one trophic level to the next.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think egestion and excretion mean the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact egestion is passing out undigested food that was never absorbed (faeces), while excretion removes waste made inside the body, such as urea in urine and carbon dioxide from respiration.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often divide the wrong way round when calculating efficiency and get answers over 100%.
misconceptions.right: In fact efficiency = biomass at the higher level ÷ biomass at the lower level × 100. It must always be less than 100%.

realWorld: Eating crops directly feeds more people per hectare than feeding the crops to animals and eating the meat, because a whole trophic level of biomass loss is avoided.
Livestock farmers try to improve the efficiency of biomass transfer to their animals, for example by keeping them warm and limiting movement so less glucose is used in respiration.
Conservation of large predators such as tigers needs very large areas, because so little biomass reaches the top of the food chain.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic (the 1% and 10% figures, causes of biomass loss and efficiency calculations) is in separate Biology (8461) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: Always write the efficiency equation, substitute numbers, then give the answer with a % sign. Check the answer is below 100%.
Name specific losses for full marks: faeces (egestion), urea and water in urine, carbon dioxide and water from respiration. 'Energy is lost' alone usually scores nothing.
Make sure both biomass values are in the same units (g or kg) before dividing.
When asked how biomass loss affects numbers of organisms, link it: less biomass at each level, so fewer organisms can be supported at higher levels.
summary: Producers transfer about 1% of incident light energy by photosynthesis.
About 10% of biomass passes from each trophic level to the next.
Some ingested material is egested as faeces; it is never absorbed.
Absorbed material is lost as carbon dioxide and water (respiration) and water and urea (urine).
Large amounts of glucose are used in respiration instead of making new biomass.
Less biomass at higher levels means fewer organisms can be supported there.

What happens to ingested material that is not absorbed?
Which waste products of respiration are lost from organisms?
Which waste products are lost in urine?
Why does much absorbed glucose not become new biomass?
flashcards.back: Large amounts are used in respiration to release energy.

flashcards.front: Equation for efficiency of biomass transfer?
flashcards.back: Biomass transferred to the next level ÷ biomass available at the previous level × 100.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of the biomass at one trophic level is transferred to the level above?
markScheme: 1 mark: 10%
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of the biomass passes to the next level. About 1% is the proportion of incident light energy transferred by producers, and 90% is roughly the amount lost.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of the incident energy from light do producers transfer for photosynthesis?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1%
questions.explanation: Producers transfer only about 1% of the incident light energy. The 10% figure refers to biomass transferred between trophic levels.

questions.question: Material that is eaten but not absorbed leaves an animal's body as:
markScheme: 1 mark: faeces
questions.explanation: Undigested, unabsorbed food is egested as faeces. Urine and carbon dioxide are waste products made after absorption.

questions.question: Which waste products of respiration are lost from an animal, reducing the biomass passed on?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide and water
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water. Urea is lost in urine, glucose and oxygen are reactants, and faeces are egested.

questions.question: Some absorbed material is lost from an animal in its urine. Which substances are lost in this way?
markScheme: 1 mark: water and urea
questions.explanation: Urine contains water and urea. Undigested cellulose is egested in faeces, and carbon dioxide is breathed out.

questions.question: Large amounts of the glucose absorbed by an animal do not become new biomass. Which process uses this glucose?
markScheme: 1 mark: respiration
questions.explanation: Glucose is used in respiration to release energy for life processes. Animals do not photosynthesise, and egestion and digestion do not use up absorbed glucose.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why there are usually fewer organisms at higher trophic levels?
options: Organisms at higher levels are always larger
Less biomass is available at each higher level, so fewer organisms can be supported
Organisms at higher levels reproduce more slowly
Organisms at higher levels are eaten by decomposers
markScheme: 1 mark: less biomass is available at each higher level, so fewer organisms can be supported
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of biomass passes up each level, so higher levels have much less biomass to support a population. Body size and reproduction rate do not explain the general pattern.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a way biomass is lost between trophic levels?
markScheme: 1 mark: photosynthesis by producers
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis makes biomass rather than losing it. Egestion, respiration and excretion of urea all remove material that could otherwise have been passed on.

questions.question: Why can a hectare of wheat feed more people if they eat the wheat directly than if the wheat is fed to cattle and people eat the beef?
options: Wheat contains more protein than beef
Eating the wheat removes a trophic level, so less biomass is lost
Beef is digested less efficiently by humans
markScheme: 1 mark: eating the wheat removes a trophic level, so less biomass is lost
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of the wheat biomass becomes cattle biomass. Eating wheat directly avoids that loss. Cattle do not photosynthesise at all, and the protein content is not the reason.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass of the producers and the primary consumers in a habitat.
Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer from the producers to the primary consumers.
markScheme: 1 mark: 10%
questions.explanation: Efficiency = biomass transferred ÷ biomass available × 100 = 500 ÷ 5000 × 100 = 10%.

questions.question:
Rabbits feed on the grass in a field.
Table 1 shows the biomass of the grass and the biomass of the rabbits.
Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer from the grass to the rabbits.
markScheme: 1 mark: 9%

questions.question:
A young cow eats grass.
Table 1 shows the mass of grass the cow eats in one day and the increase in the cow's body mass on that day.
Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer from the grass to the cow.

headers: Mass of grass eaten in kg
Increase in body mass in kg

markScheme: 1 mark: 4%
questions.explanation: 0.32 ÷ 8 = 0.04, so the efficiency is 4%. Much of the grass is egested or used in respiration.

questions.question:
A sheep eats 8 kg of grass. It egests 3.6 kg of this as faeces.
Calculate the percentage of the grass eaten that is egested.
markScheme: 1 mark: 45%
questions.explanation: 3.6 ÷ 8 = 0.45, which is 45%. This material was never absorbed, so it cannot become sheep biomass.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a pyramid of biomass for a food chain with four trophic levels. It is not drawn to scale.
Assume that 10% of the biomass is transferred from each trophic level to the next.
Calculate the biomass at trophic level 4.

markScheme: 1 mark: 20 kg
questions.explanation: Level 2 = 2000 kg, level 3 = 200 kg, level 4 = 20 kg. There are three transfers between level 1 and level 4, not four.

questions.question:
The incident light energy falling on a field each year is 2 000 000 kJ per m². The plants transfer 1% of this energy by photosynthesis.
Calculate the energy transferred by the plants per m² each year.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20 000 kJ per m²
questions.explanation: 1% of 2 000 000 = 2 000 000 ÷ 100 = 20 000 kJ per m². The other 99% is not transferred into the plants' biomass.

markScheme: 1 mark: 10%
questions.explanation: First find the biomass left: 200 − 110 − 70 = 20 g. Then 20 ÷ 200 × 100 = 10%, matching the typical figure.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass of two trophic levels in a pond.
Calculate the overall efficiency of biomass transfer from the producers to the secondary consumers.
questions.explanation: 30 ÷ 4000 × 100 = 0.75%. This is two transfers, so it is much lower than the 10% for a single step.

questions.question: State the approximate percentage of biomass transferred from one trophic level to the next.
markScheme: 1 mark: about 10%
questions.explanation: Approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above.

questions.question: Give two ways in which biomass is lost between one trophic level and the next.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: not all material is absorbed / egested as faeces; used in respiration / lost as carbon dioxide and water; lost as water and urea in urine; not all parts of the organism are eaten
questions.explanation: Each named loss is a reason why only about 10% of biomass reaches the next level.

questions.question: Explain why the biomass in a rabbit's faeces is not transferred to the rabbit's body.
markScheme: 1 mark: the material in faeces was not digested / absorbed into the blood
1 mark: it is egested / passed out of the gut, so it cannot become rabbit tissue
questions.explanation: Faeces contain food that passed through the gut without being absorbed, so it never became part of the rabbit.

questions.question: Explain how respiration in a herbivore reduces the biomass available to a carnivore that eats it.
markScheme: 1 mark: large amounts of glucose are used in respiration (instead of making new tissue)
1 mark: the products, carbon dioxide and water, are lost to the environment
questions.explanation: Glucose that is respired is broken down to carbon dioxide and water, which leave the body, so that mass never becomes herbivore biomass for the carnivore to eat.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass of the producers and the herbivores in a habitat.
Give the efficiency of biomass transfer from the producers to the herbivores as a fraction in its simplest form.
questions.explanation: 80/2000: divide top and bottom by 80 to get 1/25. As a percentage this is 4%.

questions.question: Explain how the loss of biomass between trophic levels affects the number of organisms at each trophic level.
markScheme: 1 mark: only about 10% of biomass is transferred to each level
1 mark: so there is less biomass available at each higher trophic level
1 mark: so fewer organisms / a smaller total mass of organisms can be supported at higher levels (or the chain cannot support many levels)
questions.explanation: The chain of reasoning is: losses, so less biomass, so fewer organisms. Missing the middle link loses a mark.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass at each trophic level in a food chain.
Use calculations to show which transfer is more efficient: grass to rabbits, or rabbits to foxes.
markScheme: 1 mark: grass to rabbits = 150 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 7.5%
1 mark: rabbits to foxes = 18 ÷ 150 × 100 = 12%
1 mark: rabbits to foxes is more efficient
questions.explanation: Always divide by the biomass of the lower level for each step. Herbivores often transfer less efficiently because plant material is harder to digest, so more is egested.

questions.question: Name the process producers use to transfer energy from light into biomass.
markScheme: 1 mark: photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Producers use about 1% of the incident light energy for photosynthesis, making glucose that becomes biomass.

questions.question: What is meant by egestion?
markScheme: 1 mark: passing out undigested / unabsorbed food (from the gut) as faeces
questions.explanation: Egestion removes food that was never absorbed. It is different from excretion, which removes waste made inside the body.

questions.question: Explain why only about 10% of the biomass at one trophic level is transferred to the next, and explain how this affects the number of organisms and the number of trophic levels in a food chain.
markScheme: Indicative content:
not all of each organism is eaten (e.g. roots, bones, shells)
not all ingested material is absorbed; some is egested as faeces
some absorbed material is lost as waste
carbon dioxide and water lost from respiration
water and urea lost in urine
large amounts of glucose used in respiration to release energy (movement, keeping warm), so not used for growth
so less biomass is available at each higher trophic level
so fewer organisms / smaller total mass can be supported at higher levels
pyramids of biomass get narrower towards the top
after four or five levels too little biomass remains to support another population, so food chains are short
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): several specific losses explained, clearly linked to less biomass and fewer organisms, and to the length of food chains.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some specific losses with a link to fewer organisms at higher levels.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two losses or a simple statement that biomass decreases.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The best answers use precise terms (egested, urea, respiration) and complete the logical chain from losses to fewer organisms to limited food chain length.

questions.question: A rabbit eats grass. Describe what happens to the biomass in the grass the rabbit eats.
markScheme: Indicative content:
some is not absorbed and is egested as faeces
the rest is absorbed into the rabbit's body
large amounts of glucose are used in respiration
producing carbon dioxide and water, which are lost
some is lost as water and urea in urine
a small amount (about 10%) becomes new rabbit biomass / growth
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear account of egestion, respiration and excretion losses and the small proportion becoming new biomass.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two fates of the biomass described.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Follow the biomass in order: ingested, then either egested or absorbed; absorbed material is respired, excreted or becomes new tissue.
